content: 1. Contaminated materials should be disposed of in a leak-proof, puncture-resistant waste disposal container. 2. After successful disinfection, the incident must be reported to the appropriate authority, and they should be informed that the site has been decontaminated. 3. 4. Reports of acute respiratory infections and tuberculosis transmission associated with air travel have been attributed to direct person-to-person contact, not packaging issues or shipping incidents. 5. Statistical data from central laboratories demonstrate the effectiveness of packaging compliant with P650 and P620 in ensuring the safe transport of infectious substances without leakage or material loss. Only 0.002% of total cases reported any issues, and all leakages were contained by absorbent materials without damage to secondary containers or outer packaging. 6. International transport regulations require incident reporting to both transport and health authorities, particularly for Category A infectious substances. 7. The United Nations website provides detailed information on the transport of dangerous goods, including downloadable PDFs of the UN Recommendations and the European Agreement for the International Carriage of Dangerous Goods by Road (ADR). 8. For surface transport, cultures intended for diagnostic or clinical purposes may be classified as Category B infectious substances. 9. Examples of Category A infectious substances include microorganisms such as Bacillus anthracis (cultures only), Brucella species (cultures only), Clostridium botulinum (cultures only), Ebola virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cultures only), and others. 10. Packaging for infectious substances must meet specific requirements, including leak-proof primary and secondary receptacles, absorbent materials, and rigid outer packaging. 11. For refrigerated or frozen substances, the packaging must maintain integrity at the temperature of the refrigerant used, and dry ice or liquid nitrogen must allow for safe venting of gases. 12. When infectious substances are transported, they must be clearly labeled with the proper shipping name and meet all regulatory requirements. 13. Decontaminated waste that previously contained infectious substances may be considered non-hazardous unless it meets criteria for another classification. 14. Special provisions apply to certain substances, such as genetically modified organisms, non-infectious specimens, and substances transported with dry ice or liquid nitrogen. 15. Non-infectious specimens containing small amounts of ethanol, formaldehyde, or isopropanol are not subject to dangerous goods regulations if specific packaging and marking requirements are met. 16. Infectious substances must be classified based on their risk, with professional judgment used to determine the likelihood of pathogens being present based on medical history, symptoms, and endemic conditions.
